query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, an optimal Al concentration (within a narrowly defined range) promotes a specific degree of chemical ordering that stabilizes a dual-phase microstructure (a primary FCC solid solution containing a uniform dispersion of ordered γ′ precipitates) which in turn simultaneously enhances high-temperature strength, environmental (oxidation) resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or as-deposited Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with a baseline composition having sub-optimal Al content (e.g., 5 at.% Al) exhibiting a predominantly FCC solid solution with minor or uncontrolled precipitate formation.
generation.intervention: Systematic increase of Al content in the alloy by increment steps (e.g., from 5 at.% up to about 10–12 at.% Al) while keeping other elements constant.
generation.conditions: Controlled synthesis via methods such as Directed Energy Deposition (DED) and subsequent heat treatment to achieve near-equilibrium microstructures; mechanical testing conducted at elevated temperatures (~800 °C), under irradiation simulation conditions, and at cryogenic temperatures (e.g., 77 K).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and uniform distribution of ordered γ′ precipitates (or L12-type ordering) within the FCC matrix serving as the mediator that optimizes lattice distortion and adjusts stacking fault energy.
generation.mechanism: Increased Al content drives chemical ordering by reducing the configurational entropy locally and enhancing lattice distortion; this promotes the formation of a finely dispersed ordered phase (γ′), which acts as a barrier to dislocation motion (boosting high-temperature strength), provides preferential sites for the nucleation of protective oxide scales (improving environmental resistance), acts as defect sinks under irradiation (enhancing radiation tolerance), and lowers the stacking fault energy to favor deformation twinning (improving cryogenic toughness).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, alloys with the optimal Al range will exhibit approximately 15–25% higher yield strength at high temperature, form more protective and stable Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide scales with slower oxidation kinetics, show reduced irradiation-induced defect aggregation, and demonstrate increased ductility and toughness at cryogenic temperatures due to activated twinning. All these changes should correlate quantitatively with the degree of observed chemical ordering.
generation.baseline: An alloy in which Al content is below the optimal level (e.g., 5 at.% Al), leading to a less ordered FCC solid solution with either excessive lattice instability or uncontrolled precipitate formation that compromises the balance between strength, oxidation resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with minor variations in other alloying elements; outside the optimal Al content window (e.g., below 5 at.% or above 12 at.%), undesirable phase transformations (e.g., formation of brittle intermetallic compounds or excessive precipitate coarsening) will occur, thereby degrading one or more targeted properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Al content range may vary with processing conditions and slight compositional fluctuations; furthermore, interactions with trace impurities or minor alloying additions (e.g., Ti) could confound the direct relationship between Al-driven ordering and the multi-functional property improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys: one set with the optimal Al range (e.g., 10 at.% Al) and one set with a lower than optimal level (e.g., 5 at.% Al). Process both sets under identical synthesis and post-treatment conditions. Subject samples from each set to a battery of tests: high-temperature mechanical testing (around 800 °C), oxidation kinetics measurements (at specified temperatures), simulated irradiation exposure, and cryogenic mechanical testing (e.g., at 77 K).
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM/EBSD) to quantify the volume fraction and distribution of ordered precipitates.
High-temperature yield and ultimate tensile strength measurements.
Oxidation kinetics via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and scale characterization using XRD or SEM-EDS.
Post-irradiation defect density using techniques such as positron annihilation spectroscopy or TEM.
Cryogenic mechanical properties including fracture toughness and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with increased Al content within the prescribed optimal range do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >15% improvement) in high-temperature strength, oxidation resistance, irradiation defect mitigation, and cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline lower-Al alloy, or if the microstructural analysis does not reveal the formation of the predicted uniform ordered precipitates, then the hypothesis that optimal Al-driven chemical ordering governs the multi-functional phase stability in these alloys would be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: In particular, the extraordinary ductility and fracture toughness of FCC-structured HEAs at ambient temperature and cryogenic temperatures have garnered significant attention [,,,,]. The low yield strength of FCC-structured HEAs, which is typically just 200 MPa in the as-cast form, is a significant disadvantage, as it is significantly less than the necessary strength of metallic structural materials [,]. To overcome these limitations in mechanical properties, a proposed method is to manufacture an HEA composed of a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix with an ordered FCC structure (L12) precipitated phase, i.e., the γ′ phase, by adding Al + Ti. An HEA based on a γ + γ′ alloy system exhibited excellent thermal stability, coarsening resistance, and strength retention around a temperature of 800 °C [,,,]. The γ′ phase is an ordered phase with an almost exact stoichiometric composition ((Ni, Co)3(Ti, Al)) in the Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA, with γ′ depending on the Al + Ti content []. Numerous studies have been conducted on the γ′ phase’s formation and mechanical properties [,]. A high content of Al + Ti leads to the formation of precipitate phases such as Ni2AlTi. Based on the predictive model and SHAP interpretation, a strategic approach to optimizing Al–Ti–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs for high hardness includes: (i) increasing Al and Ti contents, which are dominant in enhancing hardness via lattice distortion and precipitation strengthening; (ii) maintaining a Ti/Al ratio between 1.2 and 2.0 to favor duplex phase formation (FCC + L12 or FCC + BCC); (iii) retaining Cr and Co at moderate levels (10–20 at. 1%) to assist in solid solution and phase strengthening; and (iv) minimizing Ni and Fe content when hardness is prioritized over ductility, as both tend to stabilize FCC phases that reduce hardness. These guidelines, derived from both data-driven insights and physical interpretation, provide a practical reference for composition design under laser additive manufacturing constraints.

Wang et al. also verified LPS and characterized a rapid dendritic growth phenomenon in Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni HEA []. Guo et al. studied LPS in Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni HEA by the supercooling method. The results showed that the yield strength and elongation of equiatomic Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni alloy decreased significantly due to the inhomogeneity of the microstructure resulting from LPS []. Verma et al. studied the effect of Cu on microstructure evolution and phase formation in Co–Cr–Cux–Fe–Ni HEA systems. It was found that Cu segregated at grain boundaries []. In these studies, LPS in Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni HEA and its effect on mechanical properties were studied on a macroscale. However, the effect of phase separation on deformation behaviors was not studied. At the nanoscale, the molecular dynamics (MD) simulation performed by Tian et al. found that partial dislocation slipping dominate the initial plastic deformation of Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni HEA []. Liu et al. performed an MD study of the temperature dependence of the mechanical properties and plastic inception of the Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy []. However, neither of these two MD simulations involved experimentally confirmed phase separation.

A careful observation of the time-dependent concentration change plots for varying Al to Cr ratios shows an interesting difference between Al and Cr oxides with the rest of the oxides. The fluctuation of the concentration of thermodynamically unstable oxide (Fe, Co, and Ni oxides) is higher than thermodynamically stable oxides (Al and Cr oxides), making the lines of Figure 5d–f appear thicker than Figure 5b,c. Similar observations can be made for all the oxide concentration plots, as well. As Fe, Co, and Ni oxides are thermodynamically unstable, the formation and dissociation occur more frequently in these oxides as compared to Al and Cr oxides.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), known as multiprincipal element alloys with individual atomic concentrations of at least 5 at.%, have gained tremendous research interest since their inception in 2004 [,]. Amongst them, the face-centered cubic (fcc) class of these HEAs has been extensively studied due to their impressive strength-ductility combinations, especially in cryogenic conditions [,]. Most notable is the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi (so-called Cantor) alloy, which displays strength-ductility enhancement as temperature decreases as a result of the transition in deformation behavior from dislocation slip at room temperature to mechanical twinning at cryogenic temperatures []. This is because the stacking fault energy (SFE) is a major factor that determines the prevalent deformation mechanism at a specific temperature []. Apart from the temperature dependence of the SFE, it is also compositionally dependent []. Elements such as Co and Cr decrease the SFE while Fe and Ni increase the SFE [,,]. Hence, this is the inspiration behind the development of Fe-rich [,] and Co-rich [,] HEAs, which can access twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) deformation

papers.title: Manufacturing of Ni‐Co‐Fe‐Cr‐Al‐Ti High‐Entropy Alloy Using Directed Energy Deposition and Evaluation of Its Microstructure, Tensile Strength, and Mic
papers.system: Ni–Co–Fe–Cr–Al–Ti HEA (close analog in design strategy to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni systems)
papers.approach: Directed Energy Deposition (DED) combined with phase diagram analysis and microstructural evaluation (SEM, EBSD, tensile testing)
papers.findings: A dual-phase γ (FCC) matrix with dispersed γ′ (ordered FCC) precipitates was produced when Al + Ti were added; the processed alloy showed balancing of strength and toughness. Deposition parameters (e.g., temperature at ~1300 °C) controlled dissolution and phase formation.
papers.mechanism: Tuning the contents of Al (and Ti) modulates chemical ordering and lattice distortion, which stabilizes a controlled duplex phase (γ + γ′) that influences mechanical response.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.approach: Computational oxidation modeling using stochastic cellular automata with systematic variation in the Al:Cr and Fe:Co:Ni ratios
papers.findings: The simulation shows that at low temperatures the formation of stable oxides (α‐Al2O3 and Cr2O3) is sensitive to the precise Al:Cr ratio while variations in the Fe:Co:Ni ratio cause only subtle changes; the kinetics of unstable oxides (Fe, Co, Ni oxides) fluctuate more strongly.
papers.mechanism: The model underlines that the thermodynamic stability of constituent oxides (mainly Al2O3 and Cr2O3) is controlled by the alloy chemistry; this in turn reflects on the phase stability of the alloy’s protective scale, linking chemical ordering with environmental resistance.

papers.title: Al<x>CoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloys Enable Simultaneous Electrical and Mechanical Robustness at Thermoelectric Interfaces.
papers.system: AlₓCoCrFeNi HEA used as barrier/interlayer in thermoelectric modules
papers.approach: Interface engineering with controlled Al content in HEA barrier layers bonded to thermoelectric materials; detailed interfacial microstructural and electrical characterization
papers.findings: Optimal ranges of Al content resulted in the formation of stable, defect‐free reaction layers that delivered low interfacial resistivity and excellent mechanical stability under high-temperature aging and thermal cycling.
papers.mechanism: Adjusting Al levels governs the formation of specific intermetallic compounds at the interface; this is attributed to composition‐dependent ordering effects that also correlate with the phase stability of the HEA itself.

papers.title: Nanoindentation behavior of high entropy alloys with transformation-induced plasticity.
papers.system: Metastable dual-phase HEAs (including systems chemically tuned by elements such as Al)
papers.approach: Nanoindentation tests on as-cast and annealed HEAs with slightly varied compositions to probe local elastoplastic responses
papers.findings: Subtle differences in incipient plasticity and strain rate sensitivity were observed among the alloys; superior hardness–modulus combinations were achieved through annealing, which implied that slight variation in chemistry (hence phase stability) directly affects transformation-induced plasticity.
papers.mechanism: Chemical tuning (for example via Al additions) changes the phase stability landscape and thus alters the activation of deformation mechanisms such as dislocation slip versus mechanical twinning.

papers.title: A Synergistic Framework for Hardness Prediction and Design of High-Entropy Alloys Based on Deep Learning and Intelligent Optimization Algorithms.
papers.approach: Combining deep learning prediction with SHAP analysis and intelligent optimization to propose compositional guidelines for targeted hardness
papers.findings: Guidelines derived indicate that an optimal range of Al (and Ti) content – with a controlled Ti/Al ratio – favors a duplex phase formation (FCC + L12 or FCC + BCC) that enhances hardness without sacrificing ductility.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between lattice distortion, precipitation strengthening, and chemical ordering (directly modulated by Al content) is central to controlling phase stability and resulting mechanical performance.

papers.title: Plasticity Improvement in a Co-Rich Co40Fe25Cr20Ni15 High-Entropy Alloy via Al Alloying.
papers.system: Co-rich Co–Fe–Cr–Ni HEA modified by Al additions
papers.approach: Al alloying introduced into a primarily Co-rich system to tune stacking fault energies and deformation mechanisms
papers.findings: Al addition alters the stacking fault energy and consequently enhances deformation twinning, leading to improved plasticity at cryogenic conditions.
papers.mechanism: Al-induced changes shift the balance between dislocation slip and twinning via modifying phase stability and local ordering, thereby linking composition to cryogenic toughness.

papers.title: The Effect of Phase Separation on the Mechanical Behavior of the Co-Cr-Cu-Fe-Ni High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni HEA (with relevance to controlled phase stability)
papers.approach: Experimental investigation and molecular dynamics simulations to study how Cu-rich regions affect plasticity and strength
papers.findings: Regions with Cu segregation lower yield strength and ductility, indicating that phase separation detrimentally affects the homogeneous deformation behavior.
papers.mechanism: Localized compositional fluctuations (phase separation) change the critical resolved shear stress in different regions, highlighting the importance of maintaining a stable, single-phase solid solution—an idea transferrable to designing Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys where controlled ordering is desired.

established: Al and other alloying elements (e.g., Ti) strongly influence phase stability by promoting ordered precipitates (e.g., γ′, L12) while also inducing lattice distortion.
The formation of protective oxides (Al2O3/Cr2O3) is sensitive to the Al:Cr ratio, linking surface oxidation resistance to internal chemical order.
Mechanical properties at both high temperature and cryogenic regimes depend critically on the phase constitution and the competition between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.

approaches_tried.approach: Directed Energy Deposition with controlled temperature and composition tuning
approaches_tried.outcome: Successful synthesis of HEAs with duplex (γ + γ′) structures that exhibit improved high-temperature strength and potential for further property enhancements via post-treatment.

approaches_tried.approach: Computational modeling of oxidation kinetics under varying Al:Cr ratios
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed the dominant role of thermodynamically stable oxides in controlling oxidation behavior with minor effects from other elements.

approaches_tried.approach: Deep learning-based optimization for hardness and phase prediction
approaches_tried.outcome: Generated practical composition guidelines (e.g., targeted Al and Ti ratios) that predict formation of beneficial duplex phases.

mechanisms: Chemical ordering and precipitation (e.g., formation of γ′ or L12 phases) governed by Al (and Ti) content
Lattice distortion effects stabilizing single-phase solid solutions and influencing stacking fault energies
Interplay between diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic stability in oxide scale formation
Phase separation (or its absence) influencing localized deformation (affecting dislocation slip versus twinning)
disagreements: The role of phase separation versus single-phase chemical ordering: while some studies emphasize the benefits of a uniform solid solution for deformation, other work points to beneficial effects of controlled precipitate formation.

Competing interpretations exist regarding whether radiation tolerance primarily arises from sluggish defect diffusion or from increased grain boundary area and dislocation pinning, making it unclear which mechanism predominates in multi‑functional applications.
open_questions: How exactly does varying the Al content in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys modulate the balance between ordering (precipitate formation) and solid-solution stabilization under extreme environments?
What are the quantitative boundaries (composition, temperature, irradiation dose) over which the beneficial duplex phase or single-phase stability is maintained?
How do changes in phase stability impact the competing requirements of high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness simultaneously?
opportunities: Perform controlled comparisons by synthesizing Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with systematically varied Al content (and possibly minor additions like Ti) and testing under high-temperature, radiation, and cryogenic conditions relative to a baseline composition.

Combine in situ high-temperature oxidation and cryogenic mechanical testing with advanced characterization (e.g., TEM, atom probe tomography) to directly correlate chemical ordering with phase stability and performance.
Integrate computational approaches (CALPHAD, deep learning predictions) with experimental studies to delineate the processing–structure–property relationships regarding phase stability.
Examine the evolution of interfacial phases in bonded systems (e.g., thermoelectric interfaces) to extend insights from surface oxidation to overall alloy durability.

directions.direction: Modulate Al concentration to control chemical ordering and precipitation in the FCC matrix, thus affecting the balance between solid-solution stabilization and the formation of ordered (γ′ or L12) intermetallics.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the governing role of Al by connecting its level to chemical ordering, lattice distortion, and subsequent activation of beneficial deformation mechanisms. The evidence from DED experiments (PMC11396108, PMC12444539) supports the idea that optimum Al (often in conjunction with minor Ti additions) controls duplex phase formation which is correlated with high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness. It is also supported by oxidation modeling indicating the importance of Al in forming protective α‑Al2O3 scales (PMC9498035). The parameters are well defined and the experiments (comparing different Al levels) are feasible and highly informative.

directions.direction: Investigate the effect of cooling rate and heat-treatment schedule on phase stability via modulation of secondary phase nucleation and grain size, thereby affecting mechanical properties across temperature extremes.
directions.assessment: This route addresses phase stability through microstructure refinement and controlled precipitation. While it offers insight into microstructural evolution, it is less focused on the intrinsic chemical ordering induced by Al content. Past DED and post-treatment studies (PMC11396108) support heat treatment effects, but the design space might be wide and less directly linked to the Al-driven mechanism.

directions.direction: Study in-situ oxidation and radiation exposure effects to correlate the formation of protective oxide scales and irradiation-induced defect sinks with specific phases governed by the Al content.
directions.assessment: This approach directly tests environmental and radiation response tied to phase stability. It would employ in-situ TEM/atom probe to monitor oxide scale formation and defect evolution. The evidence (PMC9498035, PMC10254199) supports oxidation and radiation resilience being linked with stable phases, but the experiment can be technically challenging and requires very specialized equipment.

directions.direction: Develop high-fidelity atomic simulations (e.g., DFT or phase-field models) to predict how varying the Al:Cr ratio modulates lattice distortion energies and stacking fault energies, thereby predicting which phase equilibria are stable under service conditions.
directions.assessment: This direction offers an elegant mechanistic explanation that can provide quantitative phase stability boundaries. The physics is well established, and previously simulation work (PMC9498035) supports the importance of chemical composition on oxide formation. However, simulation alone may lack the direct experimental controllability required to link to the full suite of macroscopic properties.

directions.direction: Implement surface engineering approaches to stabilize or modify the near-surface phase equilibria (through, for example, a controlled oxide coating) to indirectly infer the intrinsic phase stability mechanisms of the bulk alloy.
directions.assessment: This strategy tests the environmental resistance aspect by engineering a protective coating that mimics the beneficial oxide scale. While informative regarding oxidation resistance and indirectly related to bulk phase stability, it does not directly interrogate the intrinsic chemical ordering mechanisms governing the alloy.

choice.direction: Modulate Al concentration to control chemical ordering and precipitation in the FCC matrix
choice.why: This direction directly targets the central mechanism – the influence of Al on chemical ordering (and, consequently, lattice distortion and stacking fault energy) – that governs phase stability. The connection between optimal Al levels and the balance between the FCC matrix and a controlled fraction of ordered precipitates (γ′ or L12) has been supported through DED experiments and predictive modeling (PMC11396108, PMC12444539, PMC9498035), and it offers a clear, controlled experimental parameter to test the influence on high-temperature strength, oxide resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
